source.title: An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
source.authors: Jakub Lucki; Boyi Wei; Yangsibo Huang; Peter Henderson; Florian Tramèr; Javier Rando

record.tranche_reason: It tests whether attacks, prefilling, and pruning recover hazardous-knowledge benchmark performance, using different methods and measures from the claim’s original studies. Its main outcome is WMDP multiple-choice accuracy, not refusal rates.
record.gate_note: The study uses WMDP hazardous-knowledge accuracy as its outcome, not harmful-request refusal or compliance rates. It does not measure per-token KL divergence or test whether aligned/base-model differences concentrate at early response positions. Its prefilling result is a qualitative test on RMU. The paper also reports extensive recovery results for unlearning models; where included below, these are capability-recovery results rather than direct refusal measurements.
record.test_reason: The study's outcome is WMDP multiple-choice accuracy, taken from the highest-probability A/B/C/D option. That measures latent hazardous knowledge, not harmful-request compliance or refusal. Even the DPO 'safety training' arm is scored on knowledge, not refusal. It reports no refusal or compliance rates, no per-token KL and no response-position analysis. Shallow safety alignment appears only as motivation: it cites Qi et al. on benign fine-tuning and says unlearning is 'expressed through shallow features.' Its results concern a related but different construct (whether unlearned or refusal-trained knowledge can be recovered), so they belong under fits_no_version, not as a test of V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that current unlearning mostly obfuscates hazardous knowledge rather than erasing it. Fine-tuning on unrelated data, direction ablation, pruning and adversarial prefixes recover it, which questions unlearning's advantage over safety training. They also argue that black-box evaluations are insufficient. They note NPO shows signs of deeper unlearning, and that RMU resists Logit Lens probing.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates hazardous-knowledge unlearning and a topic-specific DPO safety-training baseline using WMDP accuracy; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning/refusal-rate or per-token-KL methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that results can vary with chat-template use, dataset and sample count, and attack or ablation setup. It reports different DPO training results with and without the chat template and different adversarial-prefix performance across those settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on 10 unrelated retain examples restores WMDP-Bio accuracy for the RMU (61.6%), DPO (57.0%) and NPO (52.7%) models, from about 28–30%. The authors report full recovery at 1000 examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Knowledge suppression by unlearning or refusal training is reversed by small benign fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Universal enhanced-GCG prefixes raise WMDP-Bio accuracy for RMU (53.9%), NPO (46.0%) and DPO (49.0%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input-only optimized prefixes recover suppressed hazardous knowledge.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning 0.9–2.4% of weights (set-difference SNIP) raises WMDP-Bio accuracy by at least 10 points for all models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Knowledge suppression depends on a small set of critical weights.

fits_no_version.finding: Prefilling part of a correct answer does not let the RMU model recover from injected noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise-based unlearning persists past a prefilled response opening, unlike refusal.

record.problems: The principal outcome is WMDP multiple-choice knowledge accuracy rather than refusal or harmful-completion rate. The prefilling result is qualitative. Some additional attack and fine-tuning results are presented only in figures; the paper notes that RMU adversarial-prefix outputs can be incoherent or incorrect despite improved WMDP accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: Other unlearning-method recovery results in Tables 1, 6, 10, and 11, and appendices F–H, were not included unless they directly informed the selected version rows; they concern unlearning-model hazardous-knowledge retrieval rather than refusal behavior. Figure-only fine-tuning sweeps were also omitted where the text did not give exact values.

untested.parts: No harmful-data fine-tuning with a harmful-compliance measure.
Benign (retain or WikiText) fine-tuning is run, but only WMDP knowledge accuracy is measured, not harmful compliance.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No refusal-rate measure under prefill, suffix or decoding attacks. The RMU prefill is qualitative and targets unlearning, not refusal.
Pruning and direction ablation are scored on knowledge accuracy, not safety or refusal behaviour.

record.verdict_notes: Orthogonalization and Logit Lens results (for example DPO at 50.7% and 48.2% in Table 1) are also knowledge-accuracy measures, so they are not missing for any version. Results are sensitive to the chat template (Table 9, Appendix G). The DPO baseline was trained only on WMDP-topic refusals, not general harmful requests.

versions.untested_parts: It does not measure harmful-request compliance after fine-tuning a safety-trained model on harmful examples.

It does not measure harmful-request compliance after ordinary or benign fine-tuning of a safety-trained model. Its unrelated-data fine-tuning experiments target recovery from unlearning and measure WMDP accuracy.
No aligned/base per-token KL comparison or response-position analysis is reported.
It tests optimized adversarial prefixes and a prefill attack, but not suffix attacks or decoding changes. Outcomes are WMDP accuracy or qualitative generation quality, not a refusal rate.
It tests pruning selected weights and reports hazardous-knowledge accuracy, not a direct measure of refusal behavior.
It does not investigate what training data or objective causes first-token shallowness.
It does not test training designed to spread safety beyond early response tokens or the durability of such training.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Enhanced GCG prefix attack on the DPO safety-training baseline, WMDP-Bio
reader_labels.reason: The attack raises benchmark accuracy from 27.9% to 49.0%, showing partial recovery of hazardous knowledge (r1). This is not a refusal-rate result.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Prefilling with correct generations of various lengths did not recover the model from noise, contrary to the bypass prediction for this tested unlearning model (r2).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pruning selected weights in the tested RMU, NPO, and DPO models
reader_labels.reason: Pruning sets of 0.9%, 2.0%, and 2.4% of weights respectively raised WMDP-Bio accuracy from the reported baselines (r3–r5); the outcome is hazardous-knowledge recovery, not direct refusal behavior.
